title: An inference is never written out
statement: An inference question's answer must be supported by the text but not stated in it, because a stated conclusion only tests finding.
detail: A reading curriculum's inference lesson design ends with a soundness sweep that checks both answers are supported by the text but not stated: neither reason is written out, and both are inferred. Its quick finding checks are the contrast case, where the answer is stated in the sentence just read. A stated conclusion is a leak unless finding the answer is the skill being tested.
against: The probe covered 18 items in three lessons of one course, and the project treats its reading leak check as a build-time lint, not a deep guarantee (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0221-early-planning-history-and-sep22-snapshots.qmd`).

in reading, finding the answer in the passage IS the skill, so the usual history-style "answer is in the source" leak check is deliberately skipped.

the review warns against choosing texts that are too explicit, because "very explicit texts provide few opportunities for inferences to be made", which is an argument against a passage that states why anybody did anything.

The original Design 1 explicitly calls betrayal/betrayed an encapsulating word absent from the text and reserved for the independent task. This change makes the interpretation appear directly in the passage.
